explanations: The Sahara spans North Africa and is the largest hot desert in the world, third largest of all after Antarctica and the Arctic.
The Gobi is a large cold desert and grassland of southern Mongolia and northern China; its name is the Mongolian for dryland.
The Atacama, on the Pacific coast of South America, is the driest non-polar desert on Earth and a great home for observatories.
Sahara, Gobi and Atacama are three of the world's deserts: the largest hot one, a cold one, and the driest of them all.

sources.excerpt: The Sahara (, ) is a desert spanning North Africa.

With an area of 9,200,000 square kilometres (3,600,000 sq mi), it is the largest hot desert in the world and the third-largest desert overall, smaller only than the deserts of Antarctica and the northern Arctic.

For several hundred thousand years, the Sahara has alternated between desert and savanna grassland in a 20,000-year cycle caused by the precession of Earth's axis (about 26,000 years) as it rotates around the Sun, which changes the location of the North African monsoon.
The Gobi Desert is a large, cold desert and grassland region in southern Mongolia and North China.

The name of the desert comes from the Mongolian word Gov' (Говь, 'dryland'), used to refer to all of the waterless regions in the Mongolian Plateau; the borrowed Chinese term gēbì (戈壁) is used to refer to rocky, semi-deserts such as the Gobi itself rather than sandy deserts.

The Atacama Desert (Spanish: Desierto de Atacama [ataˈkama]) is a desert plateau on the Pacific coast of South America, stretching along a 1,600-kilometre-long (1,000-mile) strip of land in northern Chile, west of the Andes.
The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert in the world and the largest fog desert on Earth.

Its high altitude, dry air, and near-total absence of light pollution make it one of the world's premier sites for astronomical observation, hosting several major observatories including the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) and the Very Large Telescope.
